# The Keeper of Hollis Lane

The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.

At least, that was what Theo Marsh believed on the October night he finally climbed through its broken cellar window. He was eleven, and he had spent most of those eleven years hearing stories about the place. Mrs. Pruitt next door said a sea captain had hanged himself in the attic. The Delgado twins swore there was a body bricked into the chimney. Theo's mother only said, "Stay away from there, it isn't safe," which was the least interesting answer and therefore the one he trusted least.

What finally drove him to it was the music.

He'd first heard it in August, through his open bedroom window at two in the morning. It was piano music, slow and a little clumsy, drifting down Hollis Lane from the direction of the dead end. By September he'd heard it four more times. Always late, always the same melody, a tune that circled back on itself like someone trying to remember the rest of a sentence.

Nobody else seemed to notice. When he mentioned it at breakfast, his mother gave him a look and his grandfather, Pop, kept stirring sugar into his coffee long after it had dissolved. Pop had been living with them since spring, since the doctors started using words like *progressive* and *memory care*. He called Theo "Danny" half the time, which was the name of Theo's father, who had died when Theo was four. Theo had stopped correcting him.

---

The cellar smelled of wet stone and mice. Theo's flashlight carved a narrow tunnel through the dark, catching rusted paint cans, a bicycle with no wheels, and a staircase whose bottom step had rotted clean through. He stepped over it, heart thudding, and pushed open the door at the top.

The kitchen was what he expected. The wallpaper peeled in long curls, the linoleum had buckled, and a calendar on the wall still read *June 1971*. Dust lay over everything like gray snow.

The hallway was the same, and so was the dining room.

The parlor was not.

Theo stood in the doorway with his flashlight trembling. The room was *clean*. It wasn't new, because the furniture was old and the rug was worn thin in a path from the door to the window, but someone had dusted it. Someone had swept the floor. Someone had placed a jar of fresh chrysanthemums, yellow and only a little wilted, on the mantel beside a framed photograph.

And in the corner stood an upright piano with its lid open and a cushion on the bench, dented as if someone had recently gotten up from it.

Theo crossed the room on legs that didn't feel like his. He lifted the photograph.

It was black and white. A young woman with dark hair pinned up was laughing at something outside the frame. Beside her, one arm around her waist, stood a young man with large ears and a crooked grin that Theo had seen every morning of his life in the bathroom mirror.

Someone had written across the bottom in faded ink: *Ada & Walt, our first house, 1968.*

Walt. Walter Marsh. Pop.

---

Theo didn't remember deciding to sit down, but he was on the piano bench when he heard the front door.

It opened slowly, the way you open a door you've opened a thousand times. Footsteps came down the hall, unhurried and slightly uneven. Theo knew that limp. He'd been listening to it shuffle past his bedroom for six months.

Pop appeared in the parlor doorway in his bathrobe and slippers, holding a fistful of chrysanthemums that Theo was fairly certain had come from Mrs. Pruitt's front yard. He didn't seem surprised to find a boy at the piano. He only smiled, and it was the clearest smile Theo had seen on his face in months.

"Danny," he said. "You found the place."

Theo opened his mouth to say *I'm Theo*, and then closed it again.

"Your mother would've liked you to see it." Pop shuffled to the mantel, pulled out the old flowers, and put in the new ones with great care, turning the jar so the best blooms faced the photograph. "We were happy here. Two years. That's all we got, but they were good ones." He touched the frame lightly. "After the accident I couldn't stand to live here, and I couldn't stand to sell it either. So I just... kept it. Paid the taxes. Let everybody think it was nobody's."

"Does Mom know?" Theo whispered.

Pop frowned, and for a moment the fog moved across his eyes the way it did at dinner when he couldn't find the word for *fork*. Then it cleared. "Nobody knows. That was the point. Some things you keep for yourself." He looked at Theo then, really looked, and something shifted in his face. "You're not Danny."

"No, Pop. I'm Theo. Danny's son."

The old man was quiet for a long moment. Then he nodded slowly, as though a piece had clicked into place somewhere deep inside him. "Theo. Right. You've got his ears. *My* ears, God help you." He lowered himself onto the bench beside his grandson, joints creaking. "She wrote a song, you know. Ada. She played it every night in this room. I've been trying to remember how it goes." His fingers hovered over the keys. "I get the start. I always lose the middle."

He began to play. It was the melody Theo had heard through his window: slow, clumsy, circling, and then stopping where the next phrase should have been, like a staircase with a missing step.

Pop's hands fell into his lap. "There," he said softly. "That's where it goes."

Theo looked at the piano. He had taken lessons for three years before he quit, and he didn't know the song. But he had heard the opening phrase so many times this autumn that he could have hummed it in his sleep, and he knew, the way you know a word is on the tip of your tongue, where a melody like that *wants* to go.

He placed his fingers on the keys and played the beginning. Then he kept going, guessing and reaching, letting the tune fall the way it seemed to want to fall.

It wasn't right. It couldn't have been. But beside him, Pop drew in a sharp breath and began to hum, and then his hands came up and joined Theo's on the lower keys. Together they stumbled through a middle that neither of them had ever heard and into an ending that sounded like coming home.

When the last note faded, the old man was crying, but he was smiling too.

"That's it," he said. "That's close enough."

---

They walked back up Hollis Lane together just before dawn, Pop's hand on Theo's shoulder for balance. The street was silver and silent. Behind them the old house sat dark and crooked at the dead end, looking exactly as abandoned as it always had.

"You'll keep it?" Pop asked at the front gate. "When I can't anymore. The flowers, the dusting. You'll keep it for her?"

Theo thought about the Delgado twins and their body in the chimney, and about Mrs. Pruitt and her hanged sea captain. He thought about all the stories people told about the house, and how none of them came anywhere near the truth.

"I'll keep it," he said.

Some secrets, it turned out, weren't meant to be discovered. They were meant to be inherited.
